near_miss.why_not: Read the Norse instrumental cognate-object construction closely. Greek corpus search found Euripides Helena 1208, θανάτῳ / ποίῳ / θανεῖν, a similar manner-of-death construction, but its roots are not cognate with the Norse death family. Searches of Sanskrit mṛtyu + mṛ and Latin mors + morior gave ordinary co-occurrences, not an anchored counterpart. The slab partner is Plautus on the Trojan horse and has no matching construction.

near_miss.lead: Place a child on the knee: sætr / son / kne
near_miss.why_not: The slab’s Greek and Armenian knee passages do not concern a child placed on a lap. Wider searches found Odyssey 19.401 and an Irish child at Conchobar’s knee; these are recorded as an outside-slab lead. The indexed Indo-Iranian knee hits concern posture/anatomy, not child reception.

near_miss.lead: ausa + water versus Greek ἀφύσσω + water
near_miss.why_not: Exact cognate material *h₂ews- and *wodr̥, but Norse ausit takes the child as object and vatne as instrumental in a naming/sprinkling scene; Homer has drawing water as provisions or for use at sea, with water as object. Wider ἀφύσσω search shows drawing wine and other uses, not the same child-naming act. The ordinary liquid-handling collocation and altered argument structure do not establish inherited ritual wording.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_11_Agathangelos ed. page 1561 - PDF page 267 (word id 46592) (w4/4)
near_miss.lead: A beloved person as the sweet light of one’s eyes
near_miss.why_not: The Njáls saga partner describes extinguishing the sweetest light of the speaker’s eyes. The Armenian partner has a spring/source of light, not the same bereavement image. Greek searches found γλυκερὸν / φάος at Odyssey 16.23 and 17.41, welcoming Telemachus, but Greek sweetness/light words are not cognate with Norse sǿtr/ljós. This appealing metaphor alone cannot establish PIE wording; Christian influence on the medieval image remains possible.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 712 - PDF page 192 (word id 31589) (w1/3)
near_miss.lead: Know/recognize by the eyes versus see with the eyes
near_miss.why_not: Norse kænna augu recognizes a predecessor’s eyes in another man; Latin oculis uidi is an instrumental of personal sight, and Armenian recognition by face/name is distinct again. These are different syntactic relations and situations, not one inherited cognition formula.

Norse sværða song suggests a battle-noise metaphor, whereas the Greek partner’s ὀμφῇ is a divine utterance. Searches of Old English song/sing forms and Latin cano + arma did not produce a cross-branch sword-song counterpart. Old English armor/horn sounds alone are same-branch parallels and do not satisfy anchoring.

near_miss.lead: Sons and daughters in property law
near_miss.why_not: Both passages involve children and property, with cognate son/daughter and modal vocabulary. Norse regulates a wife’s challenge to marriage dispositions made with her knowledge; Rus law permits a mother to give to a daughter who supports her. Neither a matching inheritance rule nor distinctive shared syntax is present.

Norse sleeping at night is ordinary narrative, contrasted with Homer’s fixed sleepless-nights formula. The Rane scene involves vigil, but the mapped sleep noun refers to other people falling asleep, not an epithet qualifying his nights. Catullus has sleep covering eyes with rest, whereas Norse sova and huila occur in separate clauses about alternative sleeping partners. The cognate sleep/night/rest vocabulary does not yield the same inherited figure.

The Norse royal-name expression is not matched by the slab Irish passage, where naming and bringing/visiting belong to separate clauses, or by Sanskrit bharata in a name. Corpus search found a Greek name/title-bearing parallel, recorded separately. Latin Lucretius 6.372 uses passive fertur with nomine, not the same active object construction.

near_miss.lead: Branches no better than the parent tree
near_miss.why_not: The Norse proverb uses plant descent as an image of human lineage. Neither Greek slab partner reproduces the figure or the tree/branch lexical pair. A familiar genealogical analogy is insufficient without a cross-branch lexical anchor.

near_miss.why_not: Norse stor værk and Armenian մեծ / գործք share only the work noun cognately: stor is not the cognate of մեծ. The Armenian is an explicit Psalm quotation praising divine creation; the Norse describes military accomplishments. Greek great deeds/work language is generic and supplies no distinctive inherited context or syntax.

near_miss.lead: Invocation of a god for rescue
near_miss.why_not: The Norse vow concerns renouncing raiding and invoking the Christian God. Vedic havāmahe is an invocation verb related to the family behind guð, but the main Norse passage does not reproduce Vedic verb-plus-help syntax. The relevant Norse invocation lies in context and has a different verb. No distinctive phrase is shared.

Norse feet, wealth, and Vedic paśūnām, cattle, are cognate; so are bera and bibharṣi. But the Norse object is wealth being carried, whereas Vedic cattle depends on janitā and the object of bibharṣi is a soma-filled vessel. The retrieval is root co-occurrence across different relations.

search_lead.cognate: ON kné, Greek γόνυ (γούνασι), Irish glún continue *ǵónu-. ON setja and Irish suidid have the *sed- family; Greek τίθημι renews the placement verb.
search_lead.argument: A child is placed on or sits at a senior’s knee in family/royal reception scenes. Homer’s surrounding lines identify a newborn grandson before naming; Norse has the mother seat Olaf before discussing a suitor; Irish context identifies the seven-year-old boy at Conchobar’s knee. The knee gesture and verbal framing deserve comparison, but the kinship acts differ and an ordinary lap gesture remains a competing explanation. None of these searched partners is a second slab anchor.

search_lead.cognate: ON namn : Greek ὄνομα < *h₁nómn̥; ON bera : Greek φέρω < *bʰer-.
search_lead.argument: Norse bears the name/title of king; Herodotus discusses deserving the designation applied to a life, and Euripides bearing an ill-reputed name. This is the same name-as-burden/attribute construction with two cognate lexical elements, unlike the slab’s accidental name + unrelated carrying clauses. Title and reputation differ, and the metaphor is readily repeatable, so this is a lead for review rather than an asserted inherited formula.
